decisionPoints.question: Should we execute the existing tasks/phase-1-task-packet.md as-is, regenerate it from scratch via task-generator, or amend it incrementally?

options.label: Execute existing packet as-is
options.summary: Trust the pre-existing 12-task, 3-wave decomposition (Tasks 001-012) and dispatch workers against it without re-planning.

options.label: Regenerate via task-generator
options.summary: Discard the packet and have task-generator produce a fresh decomposition grounded in current SPEC.md and our chosen technology decisions.

options.label: Amend incrementally
options.summary: Keep the existing packet's structure and acceptance criteria, but layer per-task addenda for tech choices (driver, CLI framework, locking) decided in dp-002..dp-008.

pros: Zero re-planning cost; immediately actionable.
Packet already passed an implementation-readiness review per its own header.
Wave structure aligns with SPEC §32 Phase 1 acceptance.
Allowed-files lists per task already enforce scope discipline.
cons: Tech decisions (SQLite driver, CLI framework, lock backend) are unspecified in the packet, so workers will improvise inconsistently.
Some tasks bundle a lot (Task 005 bundles identify+assign+claim+heartbeat+close+conflicts+status; risk of an oversized PR).
risks: Workers diverge on driver/framework choices and Wave 1 review uncovers re-work.
Task 005 becomes a multi-day single-worker bottleneck.

pros: Fresh packet can encode dp-002..dp-008 decisions directly, eliminating worker ambiguity.
Opportunity to split Task 005 into smaller PR-sized units.
cons: Throws away an already-reviewed plan; pure ceremony if existing packet is fundamentally sound.
Adds a planning round before any code lands.
risks: Regenerated packet drifts from SPEC §34's recommended ordering and re-introduces decisions already settled.

pros: Preserves vetted decomposition while pinning tech choices.
Lets us split Task 005 only if we genuinely need to, without rebuilding the whole plan.
Cheap: amendments are a paragraph per task.
cons: Two artifacts (original packet + addenda) increases the chance a worker reads only one.
Requires discipline to keep addenda in the same place workers will look.
risks: Addenda contradict packet text and a worker follows the wrong one.

decisionPoints.falsificationSignal: During Wave 1 gate-review, two or more workers ship inconsistent infrastructure choices (e.g. one uses Cobra and another uses urfave/cli, or driver imports differ across packages) traceable to ambiguity that an addendum or regeneration would have prevented.
decisionPoints.devilsAdvocateNotes: Oracle dispatch is unavailable in this planning context (no subagent tool exposed; only Read/Grep/Write). Synthesized adversarial critique: option (a) optimizes for speed but the packet was authored before any code existed, so 'readiness review' is paper-only; the packet leaves driver, CLI framework, and locking unspecified, which is exactly where Wave 1 review tends to bounce work. Option (b) is overkill because §34 ordering is sound and the packet's allowed-files discipline is genuinely useful. The honest devil's-advocate position is that opt-c's two-artifact risk is overstated: a single 'Phase 1 tech choices' addendum file referenced from each task header is one extra read for workers and prevents the most likely re-work. Recommend re-routing to oracle before kickoff if the orchestrator wants a stronger adversarial pass.

recommendation.rationale: Existing packet is structurally sound and aligned with SPEC §32 / §34, but it omits cross-cutting tech decisions (dp-003, dp-004, dp-006). A small 'Phase 1 tech choices' addendum referenced by each task captures those decisions without discarding vetted decomposition or paying for a full regeneration round.

decisionPoints.question: Implement the kernel in Go as SPEC §7 mandates, or deviate (Rust, Zig, or another single-binary language)?

options.label: Go (per spec)
options.summary: Honor SPEC §7. Static binary, mature SQLite/CLI/JSON libraries, fast cold start.

options.label: Rust
options.summary: Single static binary with stronger type/error guarantees and rusqlite, at the cost of longer compile times and slower team velocity.

options.label: Amend spec to allow another language
options.summary: Open SPEC §7 explicitly and pick what the implementer is fastest in.

pros: SPEC §7 already ratifies it; no spec-amendment overhead.
PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks demand low cold-start latency (SPEC §27 targets sub-20ms claim); Go is a known fit.
Single static binary supports SPEC §30 packaging unchanged.
Mature ecosystem for SQLite, ULID, Cobra, file locks.
cons: Concurrency around SQLite WAL + JSONL audit needs careful goroutine discipline.
Fewer compile-time invariants for event/payload schemas than Rust.
risks: Pure-Go SQLite drivers carry their own performance and correctness profile (see dp-003).

pros: Stronger compile-time guarantees on enums (close_outcome, conflict_policy, severity).
rusqlite is mature.
cons: Requires SPEC amendment, contradicting SPEC §7's 'Rust is out of scope for MVP'.
Longer build/test cycles slow Wave 1-3 throughput.
Cross-compilation to four targets is more involved than Go.
risks: Process change (spec amendment) blocks task kickoff.

pros: Maximum flexibility.
cons: Litigates a settled decision and burns a planning round.
Spec already lists explicit reasons (startup latency, packaging, libs).
risks: Scope creep into language debate.

decisionPoints.falsificationSignal: Cold-start `agent-ledger claim` p99 latency exceeds 50 ms on the smoke fixture under the chosen Go toolchain and driver, or static cross-compilation to darwin/arm64 + linux/arm64 fails without CGO toolchains we are unwilling to add.
decisionPoints.devilsAdvocateNotes: Oracle dispatch unavailable; synthesized critique: The strongest devil's-advocate argument against Go is not language preference but driver risk (see dp-003) and the fact that SPEC's enum-heavy event model would benefit from sum types Rust provides. However, SPEC §7 explicitly bans Rust for MVP and lists hook latency as the deciding factor; relitigating requires evidence Go will miss the SPEC §27 targets, which there isn't. Risk worth surfacing: 'Go' and 'pure-Go SQLite driver' get conflated; the language choice is fine, the driver choice is the real exposure (handled in dp-003).

recommendation.rationale: SPEC §7 ratifies Go with non-trivial reasons (hook latency, static packaging, ecosystem). Deviation requires a spec amendment and produces no benefit that materially changes Phase 1. The real risk lives in driver selection, not language.

decisionPoints.question: Which SQLite driver should the Go kernel use?

options.label: modernc.org/sqlite (pure Go)
options.summary: CGO-free transpiled SQLite. Enables true static cross-compilation with no C toolchain.

options.label: mattn/go-sqlite3 (CGO)
options.summary: Battle-tested CGO binding to upstream SQLite. Best performance and feature parity but requires C toolchain per target.

options.label: crawshaw.io/sqlite (CGO, low-level)
options.summary: Lower-level CGO binding favored for explicit transaction control and concurrency.

pros: Static binary trivially produced for darwin/linux × arm64/amd64 from any host.
CI/release pipeline (SPEC §30) needs no per-target C toolchain.
No dlopen/glibc surprise on minimal Linux containers.
cons: Performance is generally slower (~1.5–3x) than the C build on heavy workloads.
Some pragmas and edge cases (busy_timeout interaction, FTS, JSON1) historically trailed upstream.
Lock semantics in WAL under concurrency need explicit verification against integration tests in SPEC §31.2.
risks: Driver bug surfaces only under concurrent claim integration tests; late discovery in Wave 3.

pros: Reference performance and full SQLite feature set.
Most production deployments use it; well-known failure modes.
cons: CGO breaks the 'static binary' promise; requires per-target toolchains in CI.
Cross-compile from macOS to linux/arm64 requires zig/cgo toolchain wrangling.
Distributing binaries that depend on libc complicates SPEC §30 packaging.
risks: Packaging Task 011 stalls on cross-compile toolchain choice.

pros: Lower-level API can yield better pool/concurrency control.
cons: Same CGO downsides as opt-b.
Smaller community; harder to staff fixes.
risks: Worker unfamiliarity slows Wave 1.

decisionPoints.falsificationSignal: Either: (1) integration test SPEC §31.2 #3 (concurrent `exclusive` claims across processes) shows nondeterministic SQLITE_BUSY losses on modernc.org/sqlite that mattn/go-sqlite3 does not exhibit; or (2) `go build ./cmd/agent-ledger` with `CGO_ENABLED=0` from macOS host fails to produce a working linux/arm64 binary.
decisionPoints.devilsAdvocateNotes: Oracle dispatch unavailable; synthesized critique: The conventional wisdom 'pure-Go = always pick modernc' deserves push-back for a lock-and-WAL-heavy workload. SPEC explicitly relies on PRAGMA busy_timeout=5000 and concurrent writers across processes (SPEC §10, §31.2). Modernc has historically had subtle differences in busy handler behavior. Counter-argument: SPEC §30 packaging targets four OS/arch combinations and the team is small; CGO cross-compilation is a recurring time sink. Mitigation: pick modernc but explicitly add an integration test (Wave 3 Task 010) that runs the SPEC §31.2 concurrent-claim scenarios under -race with a deadline, and keep mattn behind a build tag for fallback if a real bug surfaces. This is the kind of decision oracle should be re-engaged on once we have a concurrent-claim micro-benchmark.

recommendation.rationale: Static cross-compilation across four targets (SPEC §28, §30) is the dominant packaging constraint, and SPEC §27 latency targets are not tight enough to require the C build's raw throughput. Mitigate driver risk by adding explicit concurrent-claim integration tests in Task 010 and gating release on them. Reserve mattn/go-sqlite3 as a build-tag fallback if the falsification signal trips.

decisionPoints.question: Which CLI framework should the kernel use?

options.label: spf13/cobra
options.summary: De facto Go CLI framework with subcommands, flag inheritance, generated help, shell completions.

options.label: urfave/cli/v2
options.summary: Lighter-weight subcommand framework; smaller binary, simpler API.

options.label: alecthomas/kong
options.summary: Struct-tag-driven parser; concise definitions and strong typing.

options.label: stdlib flag + custom dispatch
options.summary: Minimal dependency footprint; bespoke subcommand wiring.

pros: Familiar to most Go developers; least learning curve for workers.
Generated `--help`, `--version`, completions match Task 001 acceptance criteria immediately.
Persistent flags handle the cross-command `--json` and `--agent` patterns cleanly.
cons: Adds non-trivial dependency tree (viper-adjacent transitive baggage if not careful).
Larger binary than urfave/cli or stdlib.
risks: Workers pull in viper or pflag patterns the spec doesn't need.

pros: Smaller dependency surface than cobra.
Adequate for the 15 Phase 1 commands.
cons: Less common in 2026 hook-driven CLIs; fewer reference patterns for workers.
risks: Subtle behavior differences (flag-after-subcommand parsing) lead to bug reports.

pros: Concise; struct tags make per-command flag schema explicit and testable.
Strong typing matches SPEC's enum-heavy flag semantics.
cons: Less familiar; workers spend time learning idioms.
Less mature shell-completion story.
risks: Worker friction in Wave 2.

pros: Zero external dependency; minimum binary size.
cons: Have to hand-roll subcommand routing, help text, completions, repeating flags (`--validation` repeats), and key/value parsing.
Re-invents the wheel; consumes Task 001 budget.
risks: Hand-rolled parser bugs in repeated/positional flags.

decisionPoints.falsificationSignal: Task 001 (CLI scaffold) cannot land in a single PR because the chosen framework forces structural rework (e.g. `--validation` repeating flags or `--json` persistent flag handling fights the framework), or `agent-ledger --help` output materially diverges from the SPEC §18 command shape.
decisionPoints.devilsAdvocateNotes: Oracle dispatch unavailable; synthesized critique: Defaulting to cobra is the lowest-risk move but worth challenging on two grounds: (1) cobra's transitive deps push binary toward 12-15MB which complicates SPEC §27 cold-start (mitigation: build with -trimpath -ldflags=-s -w; verify p99 <50ms claim). (2) The SPEC's flag surface is surprisingly small (15 commands, modest flags); kong's struct-tag declaration would document the SPEC §18 surface in code more directly. The honest devil's-advocate position: cobra is the safe default, but if the team has any kong familiarity, kong produces a cleaner mapping from SPEC §18 to code. Worth a 15-minute spike before committing.

recommendation.rationale: Cobra is the lowest-risk path to satisfying Task 001's acceptance criteria (subcommand list, --help, --version, JSON/text envelope). It's well-known to most Go workers, integrates cleanly with persistent --json flags, and has battle-tested completion support for SPEC §30 packaging. Keep dependency hygiene: pull in cobra, not viper.

decisionPoints.question: Should Phase 1 ship all 15 MVP commands as the packet specifies, or first ship the SPEC §34 minimal slice (init/identify/assign/claim/record/verify) and defer the rest?

options.label: Full 15-command Phase 1 (per packet)
options.summary: Deliver init, identify, assign, claim, heartbeat, record, close, status, verify, conflicts, adopt, export-summary, gc, migrate, doctor in Phase 1.

options.label: Minimal §34 slice first, then fill
options.summary: Ship init/identify/assign/claim/record/verify as a tagged 'kernel preview' release; add heartbeat/close/status/conflicts/adopt/export-summary/gc/doctor as Phase 1.5.

options.label: Full minus operational commands
options.summary: Skip gc and doctor in Phase 1; ship them with Phase 2 packaging polish.

pros: Matches SPEC §32 Phase 1 acceptance and SPEC §18.17 MVP command matrix.
Babysitter §20 integration becomes feasible immediately because export-summary exists.
Doctor exists for Phase 2 pi adapter to call.
cons: Larger surface to test before any release.
Wave 2 Task 005 is heavy.
risks: Schedule slip on Wave 2 delays the verify contract (Task 009).

pros: Earliest possible end-to-end smoke (claim→record→verify) for dogfooding.
Reduces blast radius of any single PR.
cons: Phase 2 pi adapter cannot start without heartbeat, status, conflicts (it auto-claims in long-lived sessions).
Diverges from SPEC §32 Phase 1 acceptance criteria (which requires verify reporting unclaimed/forbidden, conflicts deterministic, etc.).
Two release cuts where one suffices.
risks: 'Preview' release sets external expectation that's hard to walk back.

pros: Trims the longest-pole operational surface.
doctor and gc can land in Phase 2 alongside packaging hardening without blocking pi adapter.
cons: doctor is explicitly listed under SPEC §30 binary requirements ('binary must support agent-ledger doctor').
gc is required for stale-intent recovery story §16.3, which pi will exercise.
risks: Phase 2 starts without recovery tools; first stale-intent in dogfood causes pain.

decisionPoints.falsificationSignal: Wave 2 review (Task 008) cannot demonstrate any single Phase 1 acceptance scenario from SPEC §32 (two agents claim disjoint files, deterministic conflict, verify reports unclaimed/forbidden, no full diffs by default), forcing slip into a Wave 3 catch-up task.
decisionPoints.devilsAdvocateNotes: Oracle dispatch unavailable; synthesized critique: The packet's choice (opt-a) is bold but defensible because the SPEC §32 Phase 1 acceptance is itself a 15-command contract, not the §34 'recommended slice' (§34 is an internal sequencing hint, not a release scope). The strongest argument for opt-b is risk reduction, but 'preview' releases historically calcify into shipped surface and create migration debt. Opt-c's appeal is real for doctor (binary works without it for hooks), but gc removal would actively hurt the pi adapter; splitting them is half a decision. Best defensible position: stay with opt-a but enforce Wave 1 review's gate on storage interfaces before Wave 2 expands.

recommendation.rationale: SPEC §32 Phase 1 acceptance enumerates capabilities only the full 15-command set delivers, and SPEC §30 calls out `doctor` as a packaging-level requirement. Phase 2 (pi adapter) depends on heartbeat, status, conflicts, gc, and doctor. Deferring would shift work, not eliminate it. Mitigate scope risk by enforcing the packet's wave gates and by splitting Task 005 into 005a (identity+assign) and 005b (claim+conflicts+status) if Wave 1 review surfaces oversize concerns.

decisionPoints.question: How should `exclusive` conflict policy be enforced in Phase 1: OS file locks plus DB state, DB state only, or DB state plus OS lock as best-effort warning?

options.label: DB state only (Phase 1), OS locks deferred
options.summary: Phase 1 detects exclusive conflicts via SQLite query of overlapping intents; OS-level file locking lands in Phase 2 with the pi adapter.

options.label: DB state + OS advisory locks (per spec)
options.summary: Implement SPEC §16.1 #11 fully: acquire OS locks for path sentinels in `locks/<path-hash>.lock` on `exclusive` claim, release on close.

options.label: DB state + best-effort OS lock with warning
options.summary: Attempt OS lock; if unsupported on platform or contended, log a warning but proceed with DB-only enforcement.

pros: Smaller Phase 1 surface; faster Wave 2.
DB-only enforcement is sufficient for cooperative agents (SPEC §4 trust model).
cons: SPEC §16.1 #11 explicitly requires OS lock acquisition for exclusive intents.
SPEC §28 calls out lock abstraction across platforms.
Defers a recovery question (what happens when a process crashes mid-exclusive claim?) into Phase 2.
risks: Phase 1 ships incomplete relative to SPEC §16/§28; review finds it.

pros: Spec-conforming.
Catches non-cooperative writers that bypass the CLI but respect advisory locks (formatters, shell scripts).
Forces the lock abstraction to be designed early, before Phase 2 puts pressure on it.
cons: Lock implementation across darwin/linux × arm64/amd64 needs care (flock vs fcntl vs syscall.LOCK_EX).
Adds test complexity (locks/<path-hash>.lock cleanup on crash).
risks: Subtle cross-platform lock bugs only surface in real concurrent runs.

pros: Covers SPEC §28 'best-effort on platforms without reliable advisory locks' clause.
Pragmatic middle ground.
cons: 'Best effort' is easy to write and hard to verify; review may demand a strict mode anyway.
Three states (locked / best-effort warned / DB-only) complicate doctor and verify outputs.
risks: Warning fatigue; users learn to ignore the lock-unsupported warning.

decisionPoints.falsificationSignal: Integration test SPEC §31.2 #3 ('multiple processes claiming the same file under exclusive') passes only because of DB serialization, not OS lock; killing -9 the holding process and re-claiming from a sibling clone (or worktree) yields nondeterministic ordering that violates the §16.1 #11 contract.
decisionPoints.devilsAdvocateNotes: Oracle dispatch unavailable; synthesized critique: The SPEC is internally inconsistent here. §4 says 'cooperative metadata' and §28 says 'best-effort on platforms without reliable advisory locks' and 'database state remains authoritative,' yet §16.1 #11 says 'acquire OS locks for path sentinels before returning success.' Reading these together, opt-c is the spec's actual position: locks are best-effort but DB is authoritative. Opt-a understates spec; opt-b over-claims. Real risk: opt-c needs explicit verify-time reporting of lock-availability in `EXCLUSIVE_LOCK_HELD` finding code (already in §19.3) so consumers know what they got. Worth re-engaging oracle on the cross-clone case (separate clones do not share advisory locks; SPEC §2 #4 punts cross-clone to post-MVP, so this may be a non-issue).

recommendation.rationale: SPEC §28 explicitly authorizes best-effort locks, and §16.1 #11's 'acquire OS locks' requirement is satisfied by attempting acquisition with a graceful degrade. DB state stays authoritative for policy decisions per §28. Implement flock-based advisory locks behind an `internal/locks` abstraction, attempt on `exclusive` claim, surface result in `verify --json` via `EXCLUSIVE_LOCK_HELD` finding (already in §19.3). Cross-clone coordination remains explicitly post-MVP per §2 #4.

decisionPoints.question: What is the right mix of unit, integration, and concurrency testing for Phase 1?

options.label: In-process unit-heavy
options.summary: Most tests run in-process against a temp ledger dir; concurrency simulated with goroutines; minimal real subprocess execution.

options.label: Subprocess integration-heavy
options.summary: Build the binary in TestMain and run all SPEC §31.2 integration scenarios as real `os/exec` subprocesses against a temp ledger.

options.label: Layered: unit + targeted subprocess
options.summary: Unit tests for everything internal; subprocess tests reserved for SPEC §31.2 #1-3 (concurrent claim semantics) and §31.2 #6-7 (worktree/clone fingerprint).

pros: Fast feedback loop; works under -race trivially.
Simpler CI.
cons: Goroutine-based 'concurrent processes' don't exercise SQLite cross-process busy semantics or OS lock cross-process semantics.
Misses the exact failure modes most likely to bite Phase 2 dogfood.
risks: False confidence; cross-process bugs surface in pi adapter Phase 2.

pros: Highest fidelity to actual deployment.
Validates packaging outputs end-to-end.
cons: Slow; binary build per test session; flaky on CI under load.
Hard to debug (need binary log capture).
risks: CI duration grows; race-condition flakes erode trust.

pros: Honors SPEC §31.2 #3 (concurrent processes claiming same file under exclusive) which only subprocess tests can validate.
Keeps the bulk of tests fast.
Targets exactly the failure modes a pure-Go SQLite driver might surface.
cons: Two test idioms in the codebase requires worker discipline.
TestMain binary build adds a one-time fixture cost.
risks: Subprocess tests skipped in -short mode and rot.

decisionPoints.falsificationSignal: Phase 2 pi-adapter dogfood produces a stale-intent or duplicate-exclusive bug whose minimal repro is two real processes, and no Phase 1 test would have caught it.
decisionPoints.devilsAdvocateNotes: Oracle dispatch unavailable; synthesized critique: SPEC §31.2 explicitly enumerates 8 integration scenarios, and at least scenarios #1, #2, #3, #4, #6, #7, #8 require either real subprocesses or filesystem-level setup (separate clones, worktrees, killed heartbeats). Opt-a will visibly fail to honor §31.2. Opt-b is overkill and will burn CI minutes. Opt-c is the only reading consistent with SPEC §31.2 as written. Push-back worth surfacing: subprocess tests must run in CI by default (not behind -short or a build tag), or they will rot. Make this an enforced gate in Task 010 acceptance.

recommendation.rationale: SPEC §31.2 enumerates concurrency and cross-clone scenarios that only real subprocesses can validate. Layered approach keeps the inner loop fast while ensuring the failure modes Phase 2 will exercise are covered. Enforce in Task 010 that subprocess tests run by default in CI without a -short skip.

decisionPoints.question: Should Phase 1 ship full release packaging (GoReleaser, archives, Homebrew tap, signed checksums) or a minimal Makefile + CI smoke?

options.label: Full GoReleaser + Homebrew tap
options.summary: Configure goreleaser for darwin/linux × arm64/amd64 archives, checksums, draft GitHub release, and Homebrew formula.

options.label: Minimal Makefile + CI test/build
options.summary: `make build` cross-compiles to four targets locally; CI runs fmt, vet, test, build; release archives produced manually for the first cut.

options.label: GoReleaser config without publishing
options.summary: Land .goreleaser.yaml that produces archives and checksums on `release --snapshot`, but defer Homebrew and signing to Phase 5.

pros: Phase 1 ends with shipping artifacts users can install.
Forces packaging issues (CGO, version metadata) to surface immediately.
cons: Homebrew tap setup adds out-of-band work (tap repo, GH PAT) that SPEC §30 includes but does not deadline.
Signing is a Phase 5 hardening item per §32 Phase 5.
risks: Tap repo and signing credentials block release on out-of-band setup.

pros: Smallest Phase 1 surface; matches Task 011 'release archive prep can run locally without publishing'.
Defers credential management.
cons: First real release later requires writing the goreleaser config under deadline.
Manual archives are error-prone (forgotten checksums, wrong ldflags).
risks: First release is rougher than it needed to be.

pros: Snapshot mode lets CI exercise full packaging on every PR without publishing.
Catches CGO/static-link surprises early.
Does not block on tap or signing credentials.
Matches Task 011 acceptance verbatim.
cons: Two-step path to first published release.
Tap/signing decisions deferred to Phase 5 per §32.
risks: Defer-and-forget; tap never lands.

decisionPoints.falsificationSignal: Task 011 acceptance ('release archive prep can run locally without publishing', 'CI workflow requires no secrets') cannot be met because the chosen approach demands GH PAT, signing keys, or a tap repo before Phase 1 close.
decisionPoints.devilsAdvocateNotes: Oracle dispatch unavailable; synthesized critique: Task 011 acceptance explicitly says 'release archive prep can run locally without publishing' and 'CI workflow requires no secrets'. Opt-a violates this on its face (Homebrew tap requires a PAT). Opt-b under-delivers on 'static-friendly build config' verification. Opt-c is the only option that maps cleanly to the packet's stated acceptance. The real devil's-advocate concern is opt-c's risk of 'defer-and-forget'; mitigate by filing a Phase 5 hardening ticket for tap+signing at the moment opt-c lands, so it isn't lost.

recommendation.rationale: Aligns with Task 011 acceptance criteria as written (no secrets, local-only release prep, static binary verification). Snapshot-mode goreleaser exercises packaging in CI without publishing infrastructure, catches CGO regressions, and leaves Homebrew tap and signing to Phase 5 hardening per SPEC §32. File a Phase 5 backlog item for tap + signing at the moment this lands.
